items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: He was responsible for Con Basie's theme song, One O'Clock Jump. He wrote that and Basie went ahead and like the other people done, just went ahead and said, it's his number, but it's actually Buster Smith song. I didn't know.

ctx.x: When you once told me there was a Buster Biel in Texas, it was not the same guy that was with Henderson. No, it was different. That may be the same name. I just wondered if he used strange harmonies or Buster Smith, you know, they compare him with Charlie Parker and all that.

Well, not that type of playing, no, but he was a fantastic musician as far as tonation and knowing his instrument because he could also do good arranging. He was responsible for Con Basie's theme song, One O'Clock Jump. He wrote that and Basie went ahead and like the other people done, just went ahead and said, it's his number, but it's actually Buster Smith song. I didn't know. That's right. Well, I see in those days, Con Basie was around there with the Blue Devils. Oakland

Okay, it's going on the third real of Don Alba. It's August the 6th, 1973. Day after your birthday, huh? Day after your birthday, that's right. Let me see, we were talking back there about Buster Smith and all that. What about Chalk? Did I ever ask you about Chalk? Drinking Chalk? Did you ever hear of that? Chalk houses?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: And of course, from there came the Count Basie band.

ctx.x: What bands were famous for their riffs then?

Well, most all bands. All of them set their riffs. The Blue Devils, which was Ben and Morton's band, great riff band. And of course, from there came the Count Basie band. And you had Lansford, my band, Andy Craig, T Holder, Troy Floyd, Trent. Now Trent was a little more sophisticated band, something on the P-Rong style band. Played mostly the high class hotels and schools and colleges in those days. But they also played a lot of gigs, outside gigs. It was one of these real fine, classy bands, Trent was. Troy was…
I know some of the guys that work for C.G. Khan, and maybe we should ask them.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: No, I never cut with them. That was Count Basie was in there and I remember the band real well because I was with Troy's band and we had competition there.

ctx.x: That was... Were you on that record?

No, I never cut with them. That was Count Basie was in there and I remember the band real well because I was with Troy's band and we had competition there. So, I would stay in my backyard as they say unless I was really needed.

They only cut that one record under that name. That's all. Walter Page and these Blue Devils. Blue Devils. That's correct. Yeah. I had that record at one time, Bill, and it ended up in Baker's collection.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-05-27
items.q: And Basie was the pianist in this band.

ctx.x: Well now you're talking about blues and Judy Williams and all that. Did you know Lips Fades when you were in fact?

Lips and I played together. Lips came to Dallas, Texas in 1926 with Benny Moulton's Blue Devils. And Basie was the pianist in this band. And Oren Page was the bass. So they thought that Lips Page and Oren and the Brothers weren't even related. And Page and I, we used to go out at night and sit out and play with each other. And Compton with John on the piano.
Well what about his style then? Beautiful. Great style. Did he sound the same as he did on the record with, say, LATER in 32?
